text: Because in our Puranas, serpents are not merely snakes.
They are connected to the deep realms of creation, the waters, the foundation of the earth, and hidden subtle energies.
Ananta Shesha — In the Bhagavata Purana, he is described as the great serpent holding the entire earth upon one of his thousand hoods.
This means the role of serpents is not just protection, but serving as a foundational force that sustains creation itself.
During the churning of the cosmic ocean (Samudra Manthana), Vasuki was used as the churning rope tied around Mount Mandara.
As the Devas and Asuras churned the ocean using him, divine gems along with the nectar of immortality (Amrita) emerged.
In our sacred texts, Nagas are frequently associated with waters, netherworlds (Patala), the depths of the earth, and hidden treasures.
That is why they are seen not just as creatures, but as symbols of unseen, profound forces and guardians of nature.
Therefore, on Naga Panchami, we do not merely worship a creature; we honor the hidden, deep forces that sustain creation, even if they remain invisible to our eyes.
It is also about honoring the place of every creature in nature, without causing unnecessary harm, even to one that evokes fear.
Perhaps this was the practical wisdom embedded in our traditions: by treating even a fear-inducing creature as sacred, we protected it rather than destroying it.
And by protecting serpents, they perform their role in maintaining the balance of nature.
Even though modern terms like 'ecosystem balance' did not exist back then, our ancient tradition clearly understood that every living being has a vital role in nature.
